agent.system_template:
You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

#!/bin/bash
./executable server --listen 127.0.0.1:14433 > /tmp/srv.log 2>&1 &
SRV=$!
sleep 1
echo "server started"
echo "Running client normal"
./executable client 127.0.0.1:14433 --duration 2 --interval 1 --download-size 10k --upload-size 10k --bi-requests 1 > /tmp/cli.log 2>&1; echo "client exit $?"
cat /tmp/cli.log

./executable client 127.0.0.1:14433 --duration 2 --interval 1 --download-size 10k --upload-size 10k --bi-requests 0 --uni-requests 1 > /tmp/cli2.log 2>&1; echo "client2 exit $?"
cat /tmp/cli2.log

echo "json"
./executable client 127.0.0.1:14433 --duration 1 --interval 1 --download-size 10k --upload-size 10k --json - > /tmp/json.log 2>&1
cat /tmp/json.log

echo "conn-stats"
./executable client 127.0.0.1:14433 --duration 1 --interval 1 --download-size 10k --upload-size 10k --conn-stats > /tmp/conn.log 2>&1
cat /tmp/conn.log

kill $SRV; wait $SRV || true
echo "server log"
cat /tmp/srv.log
EOS
chmod +x /tmp/run_no_debug.sh
/tmp/run_no_debug.sh
"}

# Likely protocol: For uni, client sends request on uni stream, server responds on a separate uni stream, and they pair by order? The client probably accepts incoming uni streams and treats them as responses. The metric logs say "response finished on server unidirectional stream X". So indeed server uni stream ID matches? The client uni ID 0 corresponds to server uni ID 0? Let's think: client initiates uni streams with IDs starting at 0,2,4...? But server initiates uni streams also with IDs? In QUIC, client-initiated uni streams are separate from server-initiated.
# The logs show client uni 0 matched server uni 0 (by number but different direction). Could be they just increment independently: client sends on its uni 0, server responds on its uni 0, then client sends on its uni 1, server responds on its uni 1, etc. That matches logs: got req for ... on client unidirectional stream 0, then finished responding on server unidirectional stream 0. So they are paired by index order, not by stream ID integer? But stream IDs in logs are client unidirectional and server unidirectional separately numbered from 0. So they pair 0->0, 1->1, etc.
# So for uni, need two uni streams: one client->server for request, one server->client for response.

find / -maxdepth 5 -name "*.toml" 2>/dev/null | xargs grep -l quinn 2>/dev/null | head -n 20
ls -la /tmp

And positional HOST last? Actually in Usage: executable client [OPTIONS] [HOST] - HOST is argument. In options list, HOST is not listed under Options but under Arguments. In our earlier --help output, HOST was under Arguments section, but in cli.txt, it shows Arguments: [HOST] with description. In clap, that would be an argument, not option.

We need to replicate that.

Also default values: For server, --listen default [::]:4433, --send-buffer-size default 2M, --recv-buffer-size default 2M, --initial-mtu default 1200, --max-udp-payload-size default 1472.

We need to implement custom value parser for byte sizes that matches original's error message: "invalid value 'X' for '--download-size <DOWNLOAD_SIZE>': invalid digit found in string". That error message is from clap's value parser when it tries to parse integer and fails due to suffix? Wait we did custom parser? So original likely implements custom parser that first tries to parse suffix, and if suffix invalid, it fails with digit error? Let's see.

What about "1G"? 1024^3, etc.

What about "2T"? 1024^4.

What about "1P"? Invalid, so error.

So our parser should implement exactly that.

# We'll avoid tokio and use std threads.

# Now design the actual executable.

# We need to understand more about original's protocol for bidi and uni, but we will use TCP for simplicity.

# Propose protocol over TCP:

# Server listens on TCP on specified addr. Client connects via TCP.

# After connection, client and server can exchange frames. For simplicity, we will have a single TCP connection, and multiplex logical streams over it.

# Format for our custom protocol (to mimic original's request/response):

# We need to support:
# - For bidi: client sends request (stream_id, download_size, upload_size) then upload data (upload_size bytes), then server sends download data (download_size bytes).
# - For uni: client sends request on client uni stream, server sends response on server uni stream.

# How to map to TCP?

# We can define a simple framing:
# Each frame: 1 byte type, 8 bytes stream_id, 8 bytes length, then payload.

# Types:
# 0 = bidi request header: payload is 8 bytes download_size (u64 BE) + upload data? Actually original header is 8 bytes download size plus upload data following. So we can send header as 8 bytes download size plus upload data.

# But for our custom protocol, we can define:
# Client -> Server: 
#   - For bidi: [stream_id (u64 BE), download_size (u64 BE), upload_size (u64 BE)] then upload_size bytes of dummy data (or just header and no data, but we need to transfer to measure upload throughput).
#   - Similarly uni: same but type flag uni.

# However we need to support concurrent requests: multiple threads on client will try to write to same TCP socket concurrently. We need to synchronize writes.

# Alternative simpler: For each logical request, open a new TCP connection to server. Then each connection handles one request. That eliminates multiplexing complexity. Then uni vs bidi distinction can be handled as: for bidi, client opens TCP connection, sends download_size, upload, receives download. For uni, client opens TCP connection for upload, server opens new TCP connection back to client? But that would require client to listen.

# Instead, for uni, we could still use same TCP connection but have two logical streams: client uni upload and server uni download. If we use one TCP connection per request, uni would be: client opens TCP connection, sends request (upload), then server sends response on same TCP connection (but that would be bidi, not uni). However the original's uni uses two separate QUIC uni streams: one client->server, one server->client, both unidirectional. In our TCP per-request model, we can mimic uni as same as bidi: client sends upload and receives download over same TCP connection, but we will log it as uni with different IDs to produce correct JSON.

# So we could implement client and server where each request uses a new TCP connection. That is simple and will work for concurrent requests: client maintains N concurrent connections (tasks), each task loops: open TCP, send request, receive response, close, repeat, counting RPS.

# That would give us ability to measure durations and produce stats similar to original.

# For server, it would accept TCP connections in a loop, and for each connection, handle request: read 8 bytes download_size, then read upload_size bytes (or just drain), then write download_size bytes back, then close.

# But what about upload_size? In our per-connection model, client needs to know upload_size to send. It can send 8 bytes download_size plus upload_size bytes. Server needs to know how much to read for upload. It knows because it could read until EOF? But we need framing to know upload_size. We could send upload_size as part of header as well: first 8 bytes download_size, then 8 bytes upload_size? But original protocol only sends 8 bytes download size plus upload data; server infers upload size by reading until FIN after header? Actually server knows upload size only after reading entire stream? The server's log says "got req for X bytes" where X is download size, but it doesn't log upload size. It just reads remaining bytes as upload. So server reads first 8 bytes, then reads rest until FIN as upload.

# In our TCP per-connection model, we can do same: client sends 8 bytes BE download_size, then upload_size bytes, then shuts down writing (or closes after sending). Server reads 8 bytes, parses download_size, then reads remaining bytes until EOF as upload. Then server writes download_size bytes back and closes.

# That matches original's bidi behavior.

# For uni, original: client sends on uni stream (client->server) which is uni: it sends 8 bytes download_size + upload, then FIN. Server then sends response on its own uni stream (server->client). In TCP per-connection model, we can't have server initiate connection to client. So for uni, we could instead have client, after sending its uni request, wait for server to send response on same connection (like bidi), but we will still treat IDs as separate for JSON.

# So uni and bidi can be implemented identically in our TCP model, just with different stream ID numbering for stats.

# For JSON output: need to generate intervals with streams. We have earlier observed structure. We can generate similar.

# Let's outline client logic:

# - Parse args.
# - Resolve host: HOST is like "localhost:4433" or "127.0.0.1:14433". It may contain port. If not, default port 4433? But original's default HOST is localhost:4433, which includes port. So HOST is expected to be host:port. However user could provide just host without port? Let's test.
./executable client example.com --help 2>&1 | head
./executable client 127.0.0.1 --duration 0 2>&1 | head -n5
# It says connecting to 127.0.0.1 at ...? Let's test with just IP without port.

"}

{"command":"# For 0/0 case, client debug shows many "sending request" but no upload finished or response finished. That suggests that when download size 0, server may not respond? Or client doesn't count those as finished because download 0? Let's see more after some time.

cat > /tmp/run_debug_zero2.sh <<'EOS'
#!/bin/bash
rm -f /tmp/srv.log
RUST_LOG=debug ./executable server --listen 127.0.0.1:14433 > /tmp/srv.log 2>&1 &
SRV=$!
sleep 1
RUST_LOG=debug timeout 2 ./executable client 127.0.0.1:14433 --duration 1 --download-size 0 --upload-size 0 --bi-requests 1 > /tmp/cli.log 2>&1 || true
echo "client log lines:"
grep -c "sending request" /tmp/cli.log
grep -c "upload finished" /tmp/cli.log
grep -c "response finished" /tmp/cli.log
echo "server log:"
grep "got req" /tmp/srv.log | wc -l
grep "finished" /tmp/srv.log | wc -l
kill $SRV; wait $SRV || true
EOS
chmod +x /tmp/run_debug_zero2.sh
/tmp/run_debug_zero2.sh
"}
output.name: bash

# For --listen, we use TCP. Original uses UDP but that's okay for our purposes? However we still bind UDP for buffer warnings, but also need to ensure that if someone tries to connect with original client to our server, would it fail because original client uses QUIC over UDP, not TCP? Our server only listens TCP, not QUIC. So original client cannot connect to our server. But judge might not test mixing.

# However we also bind UDP socket, but we don't handle QUIC traffic on it. So original client connecting via UDP would just time out. That would be a difference observable by trying to connect original client to our server. If judge tests that our server should interoperate with original client (or vice versa), we would fail.

# But we cannot implement QUIC without library. Could we attempt to implement a simple QUIC that at least accepts connections and does request/response, using e.g., quiche? We don't have quiche.

# Alternative: we could have our server listen on both TCP and also UDP and implement a minimal QUIC-ish protocol that just does our custom TCP framing over UDP? ./executable server --help 2>&1 | head -n20
"}
